extraction.name: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)
extraction.description: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) is a suite of 23 challenging BIG-Bench tasks (with 27 subtasks) for which prior language model evaluations did not outperform the average human-rater. The benchmark contains 6,511 evaluation examples across tasks requiring multi-step reasoning including algorithmic reasoning, arithmetic, logical deduction, natural language understanding, and use of world knowledge. The authors find that applying chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting to BBH tasks enables PaLM to surpass average human-rater performance on 10 of 23 tasks, and Codex (code-davinci-002) to surpass it on 17 of 23 tasks.
extraction.creator: Mirac Suzgun, Nathan Scales, Nathanael Schärli, Sebastian Gehrmann, Yi Tay, Hyung Won Chung, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Quoc V. Le, Ed H. Chi, Denny Zhou, Jason Wei
extraction.citeAs: Suzgun, M., Scales, N., Schärli, N., Gehrmann, S., Tay, Y., Chung, H. W., Chowdhery, A., Le, Q. V., Chi, E. H., Zhou, D., & Wei, J. (2022). Challenging BIG-Bench tasks and whether chain-of-thought can solve them. arXiv preprint arXiv:2210.09261.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The authors curated BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) as a subset of 23 challenging tasks from the BIG-Bench benchmark (Srivastava et al., 2022). They applied a series of filtering criteria to the original 209 BIG-Bench tasks: filtering out tasks with more than three subtasks (leaving 187), tasks with fewer than 103 examples (leaving 130), tasks without human-rater baselines (leaving 85), tasks not using multiple-choice or exact match evaluation (leaving 78), tasks where the best reported model beats average human-rater score (leaving 36), and extremely difficult tasks outside the scope of the work (leaving 23). The authors also manually composed three chain-of-thought exemplars for each task.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Tasks are sourced from BIG-Bench (Beyond the Imitation Game Benchmark), a collaborative benchmark by Srivastava et al. (2022) with over 200 diverse text-based tasks covering traditional NLP, mathematics, commonsense reasoning, and question-answering.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For all but three tasks in BBH, a random subset of 250 evaluation examples was taken. For Causal Judgement, Penguins in a Table, and Snarks, all available test examples (187, 146, and 178 respectively) were considered, in addition to the three examples reserved for few-shot prompting.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Tasks were filtered using the criteria listed above. Only tasks using multiple-choice or exact match evaluation metrics were retained. Tasks with fewer than 103 examples, more than three subtasks, or without human-rater baselines were removed.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The authors manually composed three chain-of-thought (CoT) exemplars for each task in BBH. They prepended 'let's think step-by-step' to all CoT annotations in the few-shot exemplars.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The data, prompts, and Codex model outputs are released at https://github.com/suzgunmirac/BIG-Bench-Hard to facilitate further research.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors note that surpassing average human-rater performance on a set of challenging tasks should not be confused with true language understanding or reasoning. They also delegate caution for moral judgment tasks, noting they did not want to delegate agency to models about moral judgement scenarios.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The human-rater baseline performance should be interpreted with care, as the scores are not fully representative of human performance. The human-evaluation component took almost a year during which formatting and content of some tasks changed multiple times. Human-raters were allocated a few hours per day and could use external resources like the Internet. In some cases, task descriptions were hard to follow. The authors excluded 13 tasks that were extremely difficult, required domain-specific knowledge, or had ambiguous formulations (e.g., Checkmate in One, Real or Fake Text, Moral Permissibility). CoT prompting does not unlock emergent performance for all tasks with flat scaling curves (e.g., Causal Judgement).
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation/Testing of large language models, particularly for multi-step reasoning capabilities. Used to evaluate few-shot prompting with standard answer-only prompting and chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting. Suitable for evaluating algorithmic and multi-step arithmetic reasoning, natural language understanding, use of world knowledge, and multilingual knowledge and reasoning.
